claims.text: The starting catalyst consists of PGM nanoparticles dispersed on high-surface-area gamma-alumina without a protective coating.
A conformal CeO2 layer thinner than 5 nm will be deposited onto the PGM nanoparticles by ALD.
Standard automotive exhaust conditions include high temperatures, thermal cycling, and reactive mixtures containing CO, NOx, and hydrocarbons.
The deposited CeO2 layer enhances metal-support interactions.
The deposited CeO2 layer stabilizes PGM nanoparticle dispersion.
The deposited CeO2 layer provides oxygen-storage capacity.
The CeO2 coating acts as a physical barrier against PGM nanoparticle coalescence during high-temperature operation.
By limiting coalescence, the CeO2 coating reduces PGM nanoparticle sintering.
Ceria oxygen storage helps maintain favorable PGM oxidation states during catalytic reactions.
Maintaining nanoparticle dispersion and favorable oxidation states increases catalytic activity and durability.
Improved PGM nanoparticle stability permits lower overall PGM consumption.
At equal PGM loading, the ALD-CeO2-coated catalyst will have higher conversion rates for CO, NOx, and hydrocarbons than the uncoated gamma-alumina-supported catalyst.
At equal PGM loading, the ALD-CeO2-coated catalyst will resist deactivation better over repeated thermal cycles than the uncoated catalyst.
The ALD-CeO2-coated catalyst will exhibit increased turnover frequency and longer catalyst lifetime.
An excessively thick CeO2 layer may block catalytic active sites.
An excessively thin CeO2 layer may fail to prevent PGM sintering.
Temperatures beyond the coating's thermal-stability limit or contaminants that react with CeO2 may negate the benefits.
Enhanced metal dispersion and thermal stabilization by similar principles have been reported in other catalytic systems.
